sub_scenario.one_line: firmware engineer: the skipped stage produced the recall

dialogue.content: I spent the first hour tidying the staged checklist and closing stale entries.
The regression pass review wrapped early today.
Compressing documentation or refactor time never bothers me.
Not all compression is equal, then.
Only the verification stage is sacred.
Someone new shadowed me in the firmware lab this morning.
A little, but the questions were good ones.
I batched my replies about the sensor timing into one message before lunch.
Before the thermostat release I ran the staged checklist and the regression pass flagged a sensor-timing fault two days before ship.
The stage caught what the demo missed.
True emergency patches with a rollback plan are fine.
I archived last cycle's notes on the regression pass and set up the new folder.
As fresh as these things get.
Our devices go into heating systems; field failures are safety letters, not app reviews.
A vendor call about the staged checklist ran long but ended well.
I walked through the firmware lab checklist with the new starter.
Careful and quick, a good sign.
Quiet afternoon; I cleared the backlog around the sensor timing.
I flagged a small inconsistency in the regression pass records and fixed it at the source.
On the compressed hotfix in March we skipped the regression stage to hit the ship date; the same class of timing fault reached the field and the recall cost a quarter's margin.
I sketched next week's plan for the sensor timing before leaving.
Lunch walk, then a clean pass through the staged checklist updates.
The ship-now-verify-later lane is voluntary this cycle.
The lane's sponsor says volunteers will be remembered when the new platform team forms.
I closed the week by updating the firmware lab handover notes.
I opted out of the ship-now lane again and my lead wants to understand my thinking. What does my history actually say?
